# Part 1: Chi-square testing using the PASeniors dataset

The tasks in this section refer to a survey that was given to a sample of high school seniors in Pennsylvania between 2010 and 2019.  The data is in PASeniors, and included in the Lock5Data package.

**TASK 1.1**  Load the data set, run the lines that filter incomplete observations, and use the glimpse command to view the variable names and types.  

How many variables and cases are there after removing those observations?

    **Response**
    
```{r}
data(PASeniors)
PASeniors <- droplevels(PASeniors |>
  filter(Preference == "Happy" |  Preference == "Healthy" |  Preference == "Famous" | Preference == "Rich") |>
  filter(Superpower == "Fly" | Superpower == "Freeze time" | Superpower == "Invisibility" | Superpower == "Super strength" | Superpower == "Telepathy")  )

glimpse(PASeniors)
```

**TASK 1.2** One of the variables in the survey asked the students to indicate which of a list of five superpowers they would most want to have.  Visualize the answers from the survey.  hint:  gf_bar(~Y, data = )

    **Response**

```{r}

```

**TASK 1.3**  Which of the superpowers was the most popular?  How many seniors chose that superpower? 

    **Response** 

```{r}
tally(~ Superpower, data=PASeniors)
```

**TASK 1.4** Test to see if the five superpowers are equally popular among Pennsylvania seniors.  Report your chi-square statistic and your conclusion in context.

    **Response**

```{r}
superpower_counts <- table(PASeniors$Superpower)

# Perform a chi-square test to see if the five superpowers are equally popular
chi_square_test <- chisq.test(superpower_counts)

# Print the chi-square statistic and the p-value
chi_square_test$statistic  # Chi-square statistic
chi_square_test$p.value    # p-value
```

**TASK 1.5**  One of the variables in the survey asked the students to indicate, if they had to only pick one, whether they were prefer to be Famous, Happy, Healthy, or Rich.  This variable is called *Preference* in the PASeniors dataset.  

Create a bar chart of this variable.

```{r}
gf_bar(~Preference, data=PASeniors)
```

**TASK 1.6**  Past preferences lead us to assume that 70% will choose happy, with 10% each choosing each of the other three. Test to see if the data in this sample lead us to reject these assumed proportions.  Carefully consider the order that R considers the different options as you write your code.

Report your chi-square statistic and your generic conclusion.

    **Response**

```{r}
observed_counts <- table(PASeniors$Preference)

# Define the expected proportions: 70% for "Happy", 10% for each of the other three options
expected_proportions <- c(0.70, 0.10, 0.10, 0.10)
observed_counts <- observed_counts[c("Happy", "Famous", "Healthy", "Rich")]

# Perform the chi-square test
chi_square_test <- chisq.test(observed_counts, p = expected_proportions, rescale.p = TRUE)

# Print the chi-square statistic and p-value
chi_square_test$statistic  # Chi-square statistic
chi_square_test$p.value    # p-value

```

**TASK 1.7** Determine which of the preferences had more students select them than you would expect from the null proportions in 1.6.  Hint:  Look at observed vs expected counts.

    **Response**
```{r}
  observed_counts <- table(PASeniors$Preference)

# Define the expected proportions: 70% for "Happy", 10% for each of the other three options
expected_proportions <- c(0.70, 0.10, 0.10, 0.10)

# Ensure the observed counts are in the same order as the expected proportions
# Assuming the options are "Happy", "Other1", "Other2", and "Other3"
observed_counts <- observed_counts[c("Happy", "Famous", "Healthy", "Rich")]

# Calculate the expected counts based on the total sample size
total_count <- sum(observed_counts)
expected_counts <- expected_proportions * total_count

# Compare observed vs expected counts
comparison <- data.frame(
  Preference = names(observed_counts),
  Observed = observed_counts,
  Expected = expected_counts,
  Difference = observed_counts - expected_counts
)

# Identify preferences with more students than expected
comparison[comparison$Difference > 0,]
```

**TASK 1.10** Perform the chi-squared test for independence to answer the research question in Task 1.8.  Report the p-value and your conclusion in context.

    **Response**
    
```{r}
contingency_table <- table(PASeniors$Preference, PASeniors$Allergies)

# Perform the chi-square test for independence

chi_square_test$p.value    # p-value
```

```

```

**TASK 2.3** Perform the chi-square test of independence in R.  What is the chi-squared statistic and the corresponding p-value?  What combination of levels is the largest contributer to the chi-squared statistic?  

    **Response**
    
```{r}
# Create the contingency table for Sporting Event Attendance and Stranger Things Viewing
contingency_table <- table(ClassData$SportsEvents, ClassData$StrangerThings)

# Perform the chi-square test for independence
chi_square_test <- chisq.test(contingency_table)

# Report the chi-square statistic and p-value
chi_square_test$statistic  # Chi-square statistic
chi_square_test$p.value    # p-value

# Find the largest contributor to the chi-squared statistic
chi_square_test$observed - chi_square_test$expected  # Differences between observed and expected

```

## Research Question: What is the average daily phone time for students living off campus?

To answer this question  you must consider only students that responded "No" to the question of whether they live on campus.  

**TASK 3.2** Create a new dataset that includes only those observations.  How many observations are there?

    **Response** 

```{r}
# Filter the dataset for students who live off campus (OnCampus == "No")
OffCampusData <- subset(ClassDataClean, OnCampus == "No")

# Check the number of observations
nrow(OffCampusData)


```

**TASK 3.3** Visualize the phone time variable for your off-campus-only dataset using a boxplot.  You should notice something very obvious.  How many extreme observations (PhoneTime>24) do you observe? 

    **Response**

```{r}
gf_boxplot(~OffCampusData$PhoneTime)
sum(OffCampusData$PhoneTime > 24, na.rm = TRUE)

```

**TASK 3.4**  Write a line of code that creates a dataset that keeps only the observations from off-campus students that have a reasonable value for PhoneTime.  Define 'reasonable' as under 24 hours.  Using these data without the unreasonable observations, what is the sample mean?

    **Response**
    
```{r}
# Create a dataset with reasonable PhoneTime values (less than 24 hours)
OffCampusReasonable <- subset(OffCampusData, PhoneTime < 24)

# Calculate the sample mean of PhoneTime for this dataset
mean_phone_time <- mean(OffCampusReasonable$PhoneTime, na.rm = TRUE)

# Display the mean
mean_phone_time

```

    
    
# Part 4: Are students that live on campus more likely to be a 'high' phone user?

**TASK 4.1** Write code that starts with the data that has no NA values, then removes the PhoneTime observations that are more than 24, then creates a new variable, HiLoPhone, that is defined to be "High" if PhoneTime is greater than 6, and "Low" otherwise.

```{r}
CleanData <- ClassDataRaw |>
  na.omit() |>
  subset(PhoneTime <= 24) |>
  transform(HiLoPhone = ifelse(PhoneTime > 6, "High", "Low"))
# View the first few rows of the updated dataset (optional)
head(CleanData)

```


**TASK 4.2** Use tally(), and some arithmetic, to calculate the sample difference in proportions of high phone users for students that live on-campus compared to students that live off-campus. The difference order should be 'On-campus' - 'off-campus'.

    **Response**
    
```{r}


# Create HiLoPhone variable if not already present
CleanData <- ClassDataRaw |>
  mutate(HiLoPhone = case_when(
    PhoneTime > 6 ~ "High",
    TRUE ~ "Low"
  ))

# Calculate the number of high phone users for on-campus and off-campus
proportions <- CleanData |>
  filter(!is.na(HiLoPhone)) |>  # Remove any NA values
  group_by(OnCampus, HiLoPhone) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>  # Count the number of observations in each group
  ungroup()

# Calculate the total number of on-campus and off-campus students
total_on_campus <- proportions |> filter(OnCampus == "Yes") |> summarize(total = sum(count)) |> pull(total)
total_off_campus <- proportions |> filter(OnCampus == "No") |> summarize(total = sum(count)) |> pull(total)

# Calculate the proportion of high phone users for on-campus and off-campus
on_campus_high <- proportions |> filter(OnCampus == "Yes", HiLoPhone == "High") |> summarize(count = sum(count)) |> pull(count) / total_on_campus
off_campus_high <- proportions |> filter(OnCampus == "No", HiLoPhone == "High") |> summarize(count = sum(count)) |> pull(count) / total_off_campus

# Calculate the difference in proportions
difference <- on_campus_high - off_campus_high

# Display the result
difference


```

## Part 5: Summarizing after grouping

**TASK 5.1** Using group_by and summarize.

Write a piece of code that groups observations by the variable TVShow, then records:

  - the number of observations in each category of TVShow
  - the average phone time of observations in each category
  - the average exercise time of observations in each category
  
You will need to copy-paste your code into Canvas

```{r}

summary_stats <- CleanData |>
  group_by(TVShow) |>
  summarize(
    num_observations = n(),                  # Number of observations in each TVShow category
    avg_phone_time = mean(PhoneTime, na.rm = TRUE),  # Average phone time for each TVShow category
    avg_exercise_time = mean(ExerciseMinutes, na.rm = TRUE)  # Average exercise time for each TVShow category
  )
summary_stats

```

**TASK 5.2**  Now make a scatterplot relating the average phone time to average exercise time, letting exercise time serve as the response variable.  

```{r}
gf_point(avg_exercise_time ~ avg_phone_time, data = summary_stats)
```
